one_liner: GPU sparse lower-triangular solve (CSR) using one thread per row; ICPP '20 reports 4.00x over cuSPARSE csrsv2.
what_it_does: Research code for the ICPP '20 paper: solves L x = b on the GPU for a sparse lower-triangular L in CSR, with no level-set analysis step. It is not a library. Each algorithm (SyncFree_csc, cuSP, cuSP-layer, our2Part, ourWrtFst, mix) sits in its own folder with a main.cu benchmark driver that reads a Matrix Market file. You would lift the kernel function out of spts_syncfree_cuda_csr_wrt.h and call it on your own device CSR arrays.
how_it_is_fast: Synchronization-free SpTRSV (Liu et al.) gives each row a whole warp and waits on per-row ready flags. Capellini gives each row a single thread. Rows are handed out in order through an atomicAdd counter. Each thread walks its row in column order, adds up the entries whose x[col] flag is already set and spins on the next one; when it reaches the diagonal it writes x[i], calls __threadfence and sets its own flag. This removes the warp-per-row waste on matrices with many independent rows per level and few nonzeros per row. The 'mix' variant has a host pass that gives a 32-row group to a warp-per-row kernel when its average nnz/row is 10 or more, and to the thread-per-row path otherwise.
when_to_use: Repeated triangular solves on NVIDIA GPUs where the matrix changes often enough that cuSPARSE's analysis phase or a level-set preprocessing step is a real cost
Lower-triangular factors with short rows (few nonzeros per row) and many rows per dependency level, the case the paper targets
As a reference implementation or starting point for your own thread-level sync-free SpTRSV kernel (MIT, about 100 lines of kernel code)
OpenCL/AMD GPUs, using the openCL/WrtFst and openCL/mix variants (tested on a Radeon Vega 11 APU with ROCm)
when_not_to_use: Matrices with long rows or few rows per level: the README says the thread-level kernels target short-row, wide-level matrices, so use 'mix' or a warp-level solver there
You need a maintained library API: there is no header, CMake target, error handling or upper-triangular/transposed solve, and the last commit was in 2021
Comparisons against current cuSPARSE: the cuSP baseline calls the legacy cusparseDcsrsv2 routines on CUDA 8-10.2, not the generic cusparseSpSV API of later CUDA versions

Modern toolchains without edits: Makefiles hard-code sm_61 and /usr/local/cuda, and open issue #2 reports a build failure in SyncFree_csc with CUDA 11.5 + GCC 11.4 (workaround: GCC 10.5 as host compiler)

integration.dependencies: CUDA toolkit (cudart, cuSPARSE for the baseline folders, Thrust headers included); OpenCL/ROCm for the OpenCL variant
integration.min_toolchain: Tested with CUDA 8.0, 9.0 and 10.2; Makefile targets compute_61/sm_61 (edit for other GPUs)
integration.platforms: NVIDIA GPUs (GTX 1080, V100, RTX 2080 Ti tested); AMD Radeon Vega 11 via OpenCL
integration.thread_safety: not documented; each call allocates and frees its own device buffers
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same CSR input as cusparse csrsv2, but a different, benchmark-shaped C function (it allocates device memory, builds b from x = 1 and times itself); you must extract the kernel and its flag/counter setup

gotchas: The kernel assumes column indices sorted ascending within each row and the diagonal stored as the last entry of every row (it divides by csrVal[rowPtr[i+1]-1]); a row without a stored diagonal never sets its ready flag, so dependent rows spin forever

Ready flags are a plain int array (not volatile or atomic); visibility relies on __threadfence plus the -Xptxas -dlcm=cg flag in the Makefile that keeps global loads out of L1. Keep that flag if you vendor the kernel

The benchmark harness does not solve with your matrix's values: change2tran keeps A's strictly-lower sparsity pattern, sets every value to 1 (unit lower-triangular), and checks the result against x = 1 with a loose 1% relative tolerance
Precision, repeat count (BENCH_REPEAT 100) and warps per block are compile-time macros in common.h (default double precision); timings use gettimeofday around launch + cudaDeviceSynchronize
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over Sympiler when the triangular solve has to run on a GPU and you have no time for symbolic preprocessing. Pick it over CSR5/merge-spmv/ISpMV only for triangular solves; those siblings are SpMV kernels and solve a different problem.
verified_claims_summary: The ICPP '20 paper abstract (reproduced in the README) reports a 3.41 GFLOPS/s average for SpTRSV over 245 SuiteSparse matrices on three NVIDIA GPUs (GTX 1080, V100, RTX 2080 Ti; CUDA 8.0-10.2; nvcc -O3, sm_61 in the shipped Makefile). That is 5.26x over warp-level SyncFree SpTRSV and 4.00x over cuSPARSE csrsv2. The README does not say which GPU or aggregation the headline ratios come from, and the paper itself was not opened.
status_note: Abandoned: last commit 2021-03-19, with one unanswered build issue from 2024. It is MIT-licensed and the kernel is small enough to vendor, but expect to update Makefiles for current CUDA/GCC versions and GPU architectures.
